story.title: FOUR KILOMETRES OF THIN ICE
story.deck: Twenty-three people breathe the last of their air under four kilometres of ice, and a rescue vessel built to survive exactly one trip.
story.shape: Rescue under a clock in six scenes: the hull's one excursion is spent on a tool instead of on seats, and the tide decides when the ice can be told no.

scenes.title: The Placard
paragraphs: *Marrow Station, surface of the moon Tavret · Hour 0*
The air clock for Halcyon was a magnetic placard on the control-room wall, and someone had been changing its digits by hand. It read 31:00. Underneath, in marker, a second number: 23.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
Halcyon sits on the ocean four thousand and ten metres below this floor. Twenty-three people, saturated at six bar, so they cannot simply be pulled up. The shaft froze round the lift cage at 03:40 and the automatic marked the cage lost. We have one vessel that can go down. Curlew, a drone-sub, six seats, nine hours to reach the shaft.
Illuminara stood at the placard rather than the screens. She had come up from the lower decks twenty minutes earlier, and nobody had yet asked her to sit.

**Imre Solano**  
The hull certificate is for one excursion to rated depth. Down and back. The lab cycled twelve test hulls and two cracked on the second excursion. I won't fly a second one, and you shouldn't ask me to.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
So six come up. Seventeen don't. I have been told to draw lots, and I would rather resign.

**Illuminara**  
What exactly does the certificate count?

**Imre Solano**  
Pressure excursions. Full cycles.

**Illuminara**  
Not seats, and not people. Then the excursion is the scarce thing, and I'd like to ask what it is best spent on before we ask who sits in it.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
It carries six. That's what it is for.

**Illuminara**  
Who says the cage is dead?

**Ofelia Brandt**  
It stopped moving, and the shaft is ice around it.

**Illuminara**  
Stopped is not dead. May I see what it has been saying since 03:40?

scenes.title: The Trace
paragraphs: *Halcyon, 4,010 m below · Hour 2*
The habitat's voice came up the cable thin and a little late. Illuminara spoke to the commander first and to the engineer second, because the commander would decide and the engineer would know.

**Marit Osei**  
I've heard about the lots. I will not run them. If someone has a plan that is not a plan to choose who dies, say it quickly, because my people are watching me listen.

**Illuminara**  
I have a question rather than a plan. Maud Okonkwo logged the cage's frame strain. Maud, there is a wobble in it.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
Sensor noise. It rises and falls, a third or so. I flagged it and wrote it off.

Illuminara laid the trace beside a second line: the moon's flex cycle, the swell and slackening of the ice shell as Tavret's orbit pulled it. The peaks of the wobble sat on the peaks of the flex, every three hours and fourteen minutes.

**Illuminara**  
Noise does not keep the moon's time. I think the cage is not held by the shaft. It is held by ice that is squeezed against it, and every time the shell relaxes, the squeeze eases. That gives us a door that opens for a few minutes every three hours and fourteen.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
Then you have the wrong picture, and it matters. The shaft is clear above and below. I put a camera on it at hour one. The ice is on the three roller carriages and fourteen metres of rack. Free those and the cage is free.

*Fourteen metres, not a plug a hundred long.* Illuminara took the correction the way she took a good measurement, with gratitude and without ceremony. It made the plan smaller. It also made it possible.

**Marit Osei**  
And you want my people to bet their lives on a wobble.

**Illuminara**  
I want them to measure it, which costs only waiting. The next peak is at Hour 6 and twenty-six minutes. If the strain does not fall by at least a third and stay down for five minutes, I am wrong, and the director's lots are the plan. I'll say so myself.

scenes.title: One Excursion
paragraphs: *Marrow Station, control room · Hour 6, 26 minutes*
Maud Okonkwo read the number aloud as it fell, and the room, which had not been quiet, became so.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
Down thirty-eight percent. Holding. Five minutes. Nine. It's coming back up now.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
So the door exists. What holds it?

**Illuminara**  
I do, partly, and I want you to hear my limit rather than guess it. At the peak I can hold the cage's weight off its rollers for eight minutes. At the trough ninety seconds. I can hold that weight or I can keep the ice walls from closing on a cut lane. Not both for more than ninety seconds.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
Seats save six and spend the hull.

**Illuminara**  
And leave seventeen with air and nothing left to come for them. A second excursion is the other road, and Imre has told us what it costs. The frame saves nobody directly, but it is the only plan with a second step.

**Imre Solano**  
Then the walls need something else.

**Illuminara**  
A frame. Four titanium struts that jack the lane open, with a hot-water lance for the three carriages. Curlew can carry it. It takes the seat bay, so Curlew goes down once, to the collar at three thousand three hundred and fifty metres, not to the habitat. It never touches a passenger. It uses its one excursion, and it comes home.
Brandt looked at the placard. Six seats were a thing she could picture. A frame was a promise.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
And if your eight minutes fail?

**Illuminara**  
Then Curlew is spent and so are we, and I will have cost you the six. I am sure of the arithmetic. I am not sure of the ice. So the first window frees an empty cage. If I fail there, nobody is in it.

**Imre Solano**  
I'll fly it once. I won't fly it twice.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
Load the frame.

scenes.title: The Order
paragraphs: *Halcyon, wet porch and crew deck · Hour 7*
The cage was rated for twelve, by weight on the rack. That left a number nobody wanted to say, and Commander Osei said it.

**Marit Osei**  
Twelve now. Eleven later. The second ride waits for more windows. Which of you goes first is our decision, not the surface's, and it is not going to be a draw.

**Anselm Dube**  
I'll propose, and you can tear it up. First lift: the stretcher cases, the over-fifties, the three who feel the cold worst. Everyone whose body gets less safe the longer it waits. They also breathe fastest, so when they leave, the air for the rest doesn't last thirty-one hours. It lasts a day and a half.

**Kofi Mensah**  
And who is last?

**Anselm Dube**  
The ones who can still work. Maud, the three of us on the rack, the commander. The people who run the place.

**Kofi Mensah**  
That isn't an order, that's a sentence. You're making the strongest wait because they can.

**Marit Osei**  
Yes. And any of you can say no to it, and nobody in this room will think less of you.

Nobody said no. Kofi Mensah, who had been younger than the argument, asked instead what the first group could do for the second. The answer was the rack: someone had to go out into the black water, at ambient pressure, with a hot hose, and clear the last six metres where the cage would land. Maud, Anselm and Kofi suited up. They would pay for it with forty hours in a chamber afterwards, and they knew the price before they asked.

scenes.title: Eight Minutes
paragraphs: *The collar, 3,350 m down · Hour 9, 40 minutes*

Illuminara had come down beside the cable, past the point where light was an idea, and the cold and the pressure meant what they always meant to her, which was information. The ice shell lay around the bore like a held breath. She could read where it carried load. She could read where it was about to close.
Curlew hung at the collar with the frame folded in its belly. Solano's voice in the water was calm and slightly hoarse.

**Imre Solano**  
Struts deploying. Lane walls at one metre. Lance in two minutes. Peak window opens now.

She took the cage's weight. It came into her like a held note, fourteen tonnes of rack and steel that the ice was trying to keep. The first carriage let go at minute two. The second at minute four. The third did not.

**Imre Solano**  
Carriage three isn't releasing. Minute five. Three left.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
That carriage has a shear pin on the east face. It's the one I always said we should replace. Hit it from the east.

Solano swung the lance. Illuminara felt the pin go, a small bright failure, and the cage dropped out of the ice and onto its own rack for the first time in six hours. She released it at minute seven and fifty seconds.

**Illuminara**  
That is as long as I can hold. If it had needed ten seconds more, it would not have been me who could give them.
The cage ran down toward the habitat at a stately two-tenths of a metre a second, empty, and the voices from Halcyon began to cheer, and she let them.

scenes.title: The Second Ride
paragraphs: *Marrow Station, surface chamber · Hour 17, 40 minutes*

The twelve rose at the second window, and she held for seven minutes and thirty seconds. This time there was weight in the cage, and the weight had names. The cage went up through the collar zone with its lights on and its stretchers latched, and then there was only a long climb in the open bore, four and a half hours of it, six bar held inside until the chamber's door mated to the cage's door and the first twelve could begin to come down to the surface pressure at the pace their bodies allowed.

The second lift took another day. Illuminara went down for the fifth window and the sixth. Each time the frame cut, she took the weight, and each time the number of minutes was a little shorter than she had said it would be.

**Marit Osei**  
That's the eleven. I'm the last one in. You can tell your director the habitat is switched off.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
Halcyon is a loss. The company will want to know whose fault the freeze was.

**Marit Osei**  
The company can write it on whatever placard it likes. Twenty-three people are in a chamber with a door.

Illuminara sat on the floor of the control room for the first time since she had come up. She did not pretend to be anything but tired. She said so, plainly, to the room, and to Solano, who had flown the hull once, as promised, and brought it home.
On the wall, someone had finally wiped off the digits. In their place, in marker, was the number 23, and a line under it.

paragraphs: *Marrow Station, control room · Hour 6, 26 minutes*

I do, partly, and I want you to hear my limit rather than guess it. At a peak I can carry the cage's whole weight for eight minutes. At a trough, ninety seconds. On glazed rack the pinions skip and the carriages carry nothing, so for those fourteen metres someone must lift all of it. I can lift that, or I can keep the ice walls from closing on a cut lane. Not both for more than ninety seconds.

**Ofelia Brandt**

**Illuminara**

It never touches a passenger.

**Imre Solano**  
Each strut is good for a hundred and forty kilonewtons. At a trough the ice leans on them with about eighty. If any one reads past a hundred and twenty, or walks more than three centimetres in its socket, the frame is finished and so is every crossing after. I read them at every trough, and nobody boards until I have read one with the cage gone.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
And if your eight minutes fail?

**Illuminara**  
Then Curlew is spent and so are we, and I will have cost you the six. I am sure of the arithmetic, not of the ice. So the first window frees an empty cage. If I fail there, nobody is in it.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
The cage runs two-tenths of a metre a second. Fifty-five minutes between the collar and us, four hours thirty-nine between the collar and the surface. Windows from 9:40, every three-fourteen. Which can we afford to miss?

**Illuminara**  
The frame at 9:40, the cage free by 9:48 and with you at 10:43. If twelve are aboard by 11:55 it meets the collar at 12:50 and crosses at the 12:54 window, and they dock at the surface at 17:40. Empty, it is back at the collar at 22:40, four minutes after the 22:36 window. So it crosses at 25:50, reaches you at 26:52, and the eleven cross at 29:04 and dock at 33:50. The cage carries eight hours of its own air. Yours, for the eleven, lasts thirty-six hours from when the twelve leave. The last window that works is 48:28.

**Imre Solano**  
Three hours to the collar, and ten minutes to deploy. The other six hours of the nine are open water and a blind dock, and we are not going there. I leave at 6:30, and I fly it once.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
Then fly.

scenes.title: The Order
paragraphs: *Halcyon, crew deck and wet porch · Hour 7*
The cage was rated for twelve, by weight on the rack. That left a number nobody wanted to say, and Commander Osei said it.

**Marit Osei**  
Twelve now. Eleven later. Which of you goes first is our decision, not the surface's, and it is not going to be a draw.

**Anselm Dube**  
I'll propose, and you can tear it up. First lift: the stretcher cases, the over-fifties, the three who feel the cold worst. Everyone whose body gets less safe the longer it waits. They also breathe fastest, so when they go, the rest have thirty-six hours.

**Kofi Mensah**  
And who is last?

**Anselm Dube**  
The ones who can still work. Maud, those of us who know the rack, the commander.

**Kofi Mensah**  
That isn't an order, that's a sentence. You're making the strongest wait because they can.

**Marit Osei**  
Yes. So here is what goes with the sentence. The last eleven choose the hour. Imre's line is the line: past a hundred and twenty kilonewtons or three centimetres of walk, nobody crosses and nobody argues. Inside it, any one of us can refuse a crossing, and nobody is carried against a refusal. The surface does not get a vote.

**Anselm Dube**  
One voice can cost all eleven of us a window.

**Marit Osei**  
A window costs three hours fourteen of our own air, which we can count. A crossing costs what it costs, which we can't.
Then she asked the harder thing as a question. The cage would land on six metres of iced rack, and someone had to go out through the porch and clear it with a hot hose before 10:40.

**Marit Osei**  
Nobody is ordered. If nobody goes, we clear it from inside the cage, which costs eighteen minutes of boarding. The first lift misses 12:54 and waits for 16:08. I am telling you the price so that you can say no knowing it.

**Anselm Dube**  
Everyone in this room owes the table three days of decompression. A body that has worked the porch owes forty hours more. Nobody should pretend that is nothing.

Two people said no, plainly, and Marit marked their names down without a word. Maud Okonkwo went because she alone knew the rack, Anselm because he had worked a porch before, and Kofi Mensah because he had asked what the strong owed the sick and had not liked the silence that followed. Maud was back through the lock by 9:25 with ice in her cuffs, and took the headset.

**Maud Okonkwo**

At 11:17, in the first trough, the struts took the ice alone, and Solano, rising in Curlew, read them off the telemetry: fifty-eight percent of rating, eleven millimetres of walk.

**Imre Solano**  
Inside. Board them.

They were aboard at 11:55, twelve of them, with the stretchers latched. At 12:50 the cage came up to the collar, and this time there was weight in it, and the weight had names. She held it across the fourteen metres for seven minutes and thirty seconds. The struts held the walls. Curlew broke the surface at 12:55, its excursion spent, flown once as promised.

The cage went on up the open bore, four hours and thirty-nine minutes of it, with six bar held inside. At 17:40 its door mated to the chamber door at Marrow Station and the first twelve began to come down to surface pressure at the pace their bodies allowed.

scenes.title: The Second Ride
paragraphs: *The collar, 3,350 m down · Hour 22, 40 minutes*

The empty cage came down the bore on schedule, and that was the trouble. It stopped at the glazed rack four minutes after the 22:36 peak, and Illuminara felt the squeeze already coming back through the ice.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
Four minutes. Say it plainly so we can stop doing sums. Can you hold it?

**Illuminara**  
Not across. I would have under three minutes and the crossing needs seven. The ice would close on the cage in the middle of the rack. The next window is 25:50.

Nobody on the cable suggested she try. Her being sure of a limit had never cost anyone anything before; now it cost three hours and fourteen minutes of air that Halcyon could count. At 25:50 she carried the empty cage across. At 26:52 it settled on the landing the porch team had cleared, and eleven people mustered at the cage door at the pace of people who could walk.

**Imre Solano**  
Trough, 27:27. One hundred and four kilonewtons, walk two point six centimetres. The line is one-twenty and three. It is inside the line, and I would let you cross.

**Marit Osei**  
Inside the line, then it's ours. One voice is enough. Who refuses?

**Kofi Mensah**  
I do. One window. The last time it read two point six it came back to two point two once it was left alone. I would rather pay in air than cross on two point six with eleven people in the cage.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
He's reading the trace correctly. It does relax.

**Anselm Dube**  
Three hours fourteen.

**Marit Osei**  
Counted. We have twenty hours of air and the crossing needs five. Refusal stands. We cross at 32:18.

They waited. At 30:41 the trough read two point three centimetres. At 31:15 the cage left the landing, and at 32:18 Illuminara took its weight, tired, and carried it across in seven minutes and fifteen seconds, fifteen seconds under what she had said. Then she rose beside it for four hours and thirty-nine minutes at two-tenths of a metre a second, a speed she found tedious and kept to.
At 37:04 the door mated. Marit Osei was the last one through it.

**Marit Osei**  
That's the eleven. You can tell your director the habitat is switched off.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
The company will want to know whose fault the freeze was.

**Marit Osei**  
The company can write it on whatever placard it likes. Twenty-three people are in a chamber with a door.

On the wall, someone had finally wiped off the digits. In their place, in marker, was the number 23, and a line under it.

scenes.title: One Excursion
paragraphs: *Marrow Station, control room · Hour 6, 26 minutes*
Maud Okonkwo read the number up the cable as it fell, and the room, which had not been quiet, became so.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
Down thirty-eight percent. Holding. Five minutes. Nine. It's coming back up now.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
So the door exists. What holds it?

**Illuminara**  
I do, partly, and I want you to hear my limit rather than guess it. At a peak I can carry the cage's whole weight for eight minutes. At a trough, ninety seconds. On glazed rack the pinions skip and the carriages carry nothing, so for those fourteen metres someone must lift all of it. I can lift that, or I can keep the ice walls from closing on a cut lane. Not both for more than ninety seconds.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
Seats save six and spend the hull.

**Illuminara**  
And leave seventeen with air and nothing left to come for them. A second excursion is the other road, and Imre has told us what it costs.

**Imre Solano**  
Then the walls need something else.

**Illuminara**  
A frame. Four titanium struts to jack the lane open to a metre, and a hot-water lance for the carriages. The struts hold the walls and I hold the weight, and neither of us holds the other's share. Curlew carries it in the seat bay; Imre began swapping seats for struts at Hour 3, under protest, as a job that can be undone. It goes down once, to the collar, and comes home. It never touches a passenger.

**Imre Solano**  
Each strut seats in a socket drilled into the collar casting, is good for a hundred and forty kilonewtons, and is rated for forty troughs. At a trough the ice leans on each with about eighty. The frame runs on its own cells for sixty hours and reads up the cable's data pair, so it does not need Curlew once it is placed. The cancel line is a hundred and twenty kilonewtons on any strut, or three centimetres of total walk in any socket, counted from installation. Past it the frame is finished and so is every crossing after. I read them at every trough, and nobody boards until I have read one with the cage gone.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
And if your eight minutes fail?

**Illuminara**  
Then Curlew is spent and so are we, and I will have cost you the six. I am sure of the arithmetic, not of the ice. So the first window frees an empty cage. If I fail there, nobody is in it.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
The cage runs two-tenths of a metre a second. Fifty-five minutes between the collar and us, four hours thirty-nine between the collar and the surface. Windows from 9:40, every three-fourteen. Which can we afford to miss?

**Illuminara**  
The frame at 9:40, the cage free by 9:48 and with you at 10:43. If twelve are aboard by 11:55 it meets the collar at 12:50 and crosses at the 12:54 window, and they dock at the surface at 17:40. Empty, it is back at the collar at 22:40, four minutes after the 22:36 window. So it crosses at 25:50, reaches you at 26:52, and the eleven cross at 29:04 and dock at 33:50.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
Air is the other clock, and it's mine. Thirty-one hours at twenty-three people. The twelve you take first are the stretcher cases and the over-fifties, and they are fifty-nine percent of what Halcyon breathes. When they go at 11:55 there are nineteen hours and five minutes left at the old rate. The eleven stretch that to forty-six and a half. Halcyon is dead at 58:27.

**Illuminara**  
The cage carries eight hours of its own air and needs under six from the landing to the surface, so the eleven can seal themselves into it as late as an hour before Halcyon dies. The last window that works is 58:10. Anything before it, we can afford to miss.

**Imre Solano**  
Three hours to the collar, and ten minutes to deploy. The other six hours of the nine are open water and a blind dock, and we are not going there. I leave at 6:30, and I fly it once.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
Then fly.

scenes.title: The Order
paragraphs: *Halcyon, crew deck and wet porch · Hour 7*
The cage was rated for twelve, by weight on the rack. That left a number nobody wanted to say, and Commander Osei said it.

**Marit Osei**  
Twelve now. Eleven later. Which of you goes first is our decision, not the surface's, and it is not going to be a draw.

**Anselm Dube**  
I'll propose, and you can tear it up. First lift: the stretcher cases, the over-fifties, the three who feel the cold worst. Everyone whose body gets less safe the longer it waits. They also breathe fastest, so when they go, the rest have forty-six hours.

**Kofi Mensah**  
And who is last?

**Anselm Dube**  
The ones who can still work. Maud, those of us who know the rack, the commander.

**Kofi Mensah**  
That isn't an order, that's a sentence. You're making the strongest wait because they can.

**Marit Osei**  
Yes. So here is what goes with the sentence. The last eleven choose the hour. Imre's line is the line: past a hundred and twenty kilonewtons or three centimetres of walk, nobody crosses and nobody argues. Inside it, any one of us can refuse a crossing, and nobody is carried against a refusal. The surface does not get a vote.

**Anselm Dube**  
One voice can cost all eleven of us a window.

**Marit Osei**  
A window costs three hours fourteen of our own air, which we can count. A crossing costs what it costs, which we can't.
Then she asked the harder thing as a question. The cage would land on six metres of iced rack, and someone had to go out through the porch and clear it with a hot hose before 10:40.

**Marit Osei**  
Nobody is ordered. If nobody goes, we clear it from inside the cage, which costs eighteen minutes of boarding. The first lift misses 12:54 and waits for 16:08. I am telling you the price so that you can say no knowing it.

**Anselm Dube**  
Everyone in this room owes the table three days of decompression. A body that has worked the porch owes forty hours more. Nobody should pretend that is nothing.

Two people said no, plainly, and Marit marked their names down without a word. Maud Okonkwo went because she alone knew the rack, Anselm because he had worked a porch before, and Kofi Mensah because he had asked what the strong owed the sick and had not liked the silence that followed. Maud was back through the lock by 9:25 with ice in her cuffs, and took the headset.

scenes.title: Eight Minutes
paragraphs: *The collar, 3,350 m down · Hour 9, 40 minutes*

Illuminara had come down beside the cable, past the point where light was an idea, and the cold and the pressure meant what they always meant to her, which was information. She could read where it carried load, and where it was about to close.
Curlew hung at the collar with the frame folded in its belly. Solano's voice in the water was calm and slightly hoarse.

**Imre Solano**  
Struts deploying. Lane walls at one metre. Lance in two minutes. Peak window opens now.

The struts took the walls. That was the arrangement, and it was a relief to be only the other half of it. She took the cage's weight. It came into her like a held note, fourteen tonnes of rack and steel that the ice was trying to keep. The first carriage let go at minute two. The second at minute four. The third did not.

**Imre Solano**  
Carriage three isn't releasing. Minute five. Three left.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
That carriage has a shear pin on the east face. It's the one I always said we should replace. Hit it from the east.

Solano swung the lance. Illuminara felt the pin go, a small bright failure, and the cage dropped out of the ice onto clean rack and its own pinions for the first time since 03:40. She released it at minute seven and fifty seconds.

**Illuminara**  
That is as long as I can hold. If it had needed ten seconds more, it would not have been me who could give them.

The cage ran down toward the habitat, empty, at a stately two-tenths of a metre a second, and the voices from Halcyon began to cheer, and she let them. She did not go up. The windows would not wait for her to come back down, so she stayed in the lee of the frame, in the dark.
At 11:17, in the first trough, the struts took the ice alone, and Solano, rising in Curlew, read them off the telemetry: fifty-eight percent of rating, eleven millimetres of walk.

**Imre Solano**  
Inside. Board them.

They were aboard at 11:55, twelve of them, with the stretchers latched. At 12:50 the cage came up to the collar, and this time there was weight in it, and the weight had names. She held it across the fourteen metres for seven minutes and thirty seconds. The struts held the walls. Curlew broke the surface at 12:55, its excursion spent, flown once as promised.

The cage went on up the open bore, four hours and thirty-nine minutes of it, with six bar held inside. At 17:40 its door mated to the chamber door at Marrow Station and the first twelve began to come down to surface pressure at the pace their bodies allowed.

scenes.title: The Second Ride
paragraphs: *The collar, 3,350 m down · Hour 22, 40 minutes*

The empty cage came down the bore on schedule, and that was the trouble. It stopped at the glazed rack four minutes after the 22:36 peak, and Illuminara felt the squeeze already coming back through the ice.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
Four minutes. Say it plainly so we can stop doing sums. Can you hold it?

**Illuminara**  
Not across. I would have under three minutes and the crossing needs seven. The ice would close on the cage in the middle of the rack. The next window is 25:50.
Nobody on the cable suggested she try. Her being sure of a limit had never cost anyone anything before; now it cost three hours and fourteen minutes of air that Halcyon could count.

The frame stood alone through the long wait, on its own cells, reading up the cable's data pair, and Maud logged every trough. Walk of 1.4 centimetres at 14:31. Two point zero at 17:45. Two point six at 20:59, inside the line. Then, at 24:13, with the cage parked above it and nothing moving, two point two.
At 25:50 Illuminara carried the empty cage across. At 26:52 it settled on the landing the porch team had cleared, and eleven people mustered at the cage door at the pace of people who could walk.

**Imre Solano**  
Trough, 27:27. One hundred and four kilonewtons, walk two point six centimetres. The line is one-twenty and three. It is inside the line, and I would let you cross.

**Marit Osei**  
Inside the line, then it's ours. One voice is enough. Who refuses?

**Kofi Mensah**  
I do. One window. Look at the log: at 20:59 it read two point six, and at 24:13 it was back to two point two with nobody touching it. I would rather pay in air than cross on two point six with eleven people in the cage.

**Maud Okonkwo**  
He's reading the trace correctly. It does relax.

**Anselm Dube**  
Three hours fourteen.

**Marit Osei**  
Counted. We have twenty-nine hours of air and the crossing needs five. Refusal stands. We cross at 32:18.

They waited. At 30:41 the trough read two point three centimetres. At 31:15 the cage left the landing, and at 32:18 Illuminara took its weight, tired, and carried it across in seven minutes and fifteen seconds, fifteen seconds under what she had said. Then she rose beside it for four hours and thirty-nine minutes at two-tenths of a metre a second, a speed she found tedious and kept to.
At 37:04 the door mated. Marit Osei was the last one through it.

**Marit Osei**  
That's the eleven. You can tell your director the habitat is switched off.

**Ofelia Brandt**  
The company will want to know whose fault the freeze was.

**Marit Osei**  
The company can write it on whatever placard it likes. Twenty-three people are in a chamber with a door.

Maud, Anselm and Kofi would spend their extra forty hours on the table without complaint. Illuminara sat on the floor of the control room for the first time since she had come up. She did not pretend to be anything but tired. She said so, plainly, to the room, and to Solano.
On the wall, someone had finally wiped off the digits. In their place, in marker, was the number 23, and a line under it.
